narrative:
The 2018 Baltimore Orioles were, by nearly every measure, one of the worst teams in modern baseball history. Finishing 47-115, they set a franchise record for losses and joined a short, ignominious list of American League teams to lose 115 or more games in a season. The collapse was total: a pitching staff that posted a 5.18 ERA bled runs at a historic rate, while an offense that scored 270 fewer runs than it allowed could never compensate. The season was less a story of what went wrong and more a story of everything going wrong at once.

The early weeks offered a few flickers of hope. Adam Jones homered on Opening Day, Anthony Santander provided a jolt in early April, and Brad Brach induced a critical double play against Aaron Judge that briefly made the Orioles look like a competent bullpen outfit. But those moments were outliers. Darren O'Day was torched for back-to-back crushing home runs in April, and the bullpen quickly revealed itself to be a liability rather than a strength. By the end of April, the Orioles were already 7-19 and the tone of the season was set.

June brought one last gasp of relevance. Manny Machado, still an Oriole for a few more weeks, delivered a towering home run, and Jonathan Schoop's ground-rule double on fan interference provided one of the season's stranger highlights. Chris Davis — so often a symbol of the team's struggles with his historic contract and batting slumps — clubbed a three-run homer on June 27 that represented the single most impactful positive play of the year by WPA. It was a brief, almost poignant reminder of what this group had once been. But the trade deadline loomed, and with it came the dissolution of whatever remained of the competitive core.

After Machado was shipped to the Dodgers in late July, the season became a long, painful exercise in endurance. The bullpen — a rotating cast of fringe arms like Tanner Scott, Paul Fry, Cody Carroll, and Miguel Castro — surrendered walk-off and late-inning home runs with grim regularity. Mychal Givens allowed the single most damaging play of the season, a two-run homer by Whit Merrifield on September 1 that carried a -0.767 WPA. The Orioles went 8-20 in August and 7-20 in September, limping to the finish. DJ Stewart's three-run homer on the season's final day provided one last, bittersweet highlight for a franchise staring down a long rebuild.

chapters.title: Flickers of Hope
chapters.description: The Orioles open the season with a few bright moments, including Adam Jones homering on Opening Day and a pivotal Brad Brach double play against the Yankees.

chapters.title: April Unraveling
chapters.description: The bullpen begins to crack as Darren O'Day surrenders crushing home runs and the team tumbles to 7-19 by month's end.

chapters.title: Machado's Last Stand
chapters.description: In June and into July, Manny Machado and Chris Davis provide the team's most impactful offensive moments before the trade deadline tears the roster apart.

chapters.title: Post-Trade Freefall
chapters.description: With Machado gone, the Orioles' bullpen collapses in late July and August as a parade of relievers surrender critical home runs in a 8-20 month.

chapters.title: Enduring to the End
chapters.description: September brings more of the same heartbreak, capped by Mychal Givens surrendering the season's most damaging home run before DJ Stewart provides one final moment of grace on the last day.
